sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Torino data is recent, so there is no city trend of our own yet. The figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026, which includes the August holidays; in August 2025 the city suspended its traffic zone and on-street charges for about two weeks [6].

Torino controls access to its centre by camera rather than by price alone. Unauthorised cars may not enter or park in the central limited-traffic zone (ZTL Centrale) on weekday mornings from 7:30 to 10:30. 27 camera gates enforce this, and further cameras guard public-transport-only streets and an area closed at night [0]. The city approved extending a second zone around the Valentino park in March 2026, with a new underground car park of almost 500 spaces planned there [1]. On the street, the 2023 tariff update raised the central rate from €2.50 to €2.80 an hour [4]. In 2026 ordinary zones cost €1.70, and residents pay €180 a year for a permit [5]. Central streets were charged on four Sundays and holidays in December 2025, normally free days [7]. A ban on older diesel cars (Euro 5) that could have applied from October 2026 was avoided through compensatory measures in the regional air-quality plan [2][3].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The municipal transport company GTT runs on-street parking across the city and 30 car parks in the centre and at the main entry points, with a park-and-ride fare. Its parking revenue was about €47.2 million in 2025, 5.75% more than in 2024 [9]. Payment has moved to phones fast. Sales through GTT's own app rose from €2.8 million in 2023 to €10.1 million in 2025, and other apps took a further €11.2 million [10]. The city has made it easier to use car parks inside the restricted zone: at participating car parks a camera is to read the number plate, removing the need for a paper permit [8].

Demand from outside is growing. GTT carried about 300 million passengers in 2025, up 4.9% [12], tourist arrivals rose 6.3% [13], and the ATP Finals drew about 230,000 spectators in 2025 [14]. Preliminary works for metro line 2 were due to start at sites in the centre in March 2026 [15]. Public charging in the province reached 3,075 points in 2025, fourth among Italian provinces [11].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Torino has the cheapest garages in our set. GTT's car parks typically charge €1 an hour and €7 a day, less than the street, which makes the car park the cheaper choice. APCOA, Parcheggi Italia and the ACI club charge more, around €1.80–1.95 an hour and €16–18 a day, and all average around 39–43% on weekdays, like GTT. The station car parks are among the dearest, at about €2.35 an hour, and the fullest: Porta Nuova at 81%, Porta Susa at 69%.

The restricted zone shapes where the garages are. Only one we measure lies within 500 m of Piazza Castello, Santo Stefano, and it is 71% full. The ring between 500 m and 2 km averages 44–47%, and garages further out about 25%. That outer group includes the 3,100-space Lingotto car park at 6% and a park-and-ride that is almost unused. Garages serving hospitals and offices empty at weekends (the Molinette hospital car park drops from 41% to 3%), while some central ones fill up instead: the Vittorio car park goes from 40% on weekdays to 71% at weekends.
